content: 1. In areas where the prevalence of syphilis is low (below 5%), the WHO STI guidelines recommend using a single on-site rapid syphilis test (RST) to screen pregnant women (Strategy A) instead of a single on-site rapid plasma reagin (RPR) test (Strategy B). This is a conditional recommendation based on low-quality evidence. 2. In areas with a high prevalence of syphilis (5% or greater), the WHO STI guidelines suggest using an on-site rapid syphilis test (RST) followed by immediate provision of the first dose of treatment if the test is positive. This should then be followed by an RPR test, and if the RPR test is also positive, treatment should be provided according to the duration of syphilis (Strategy C). This approach is preferred over using a single on-site RST (Strategy A) or a single on-site RPR test (Strategy B). This is also a conditional recommendation based on low-quality evidence. 3. These recommendations are not applicable to countries that can provide high-quality laboratory-based screening and treatment strategies. However, in settings where such strategies or sequential testing are not feasible due to resource constraints, a single on-site RST (Strategy A) is suggested to ensure broader screening coverage, even though it may result in over-treatment due to false-positive results. 4. Treatment for syphilis should be based on the duration of the infection, as outlined in the WHO guidelines for the treatment of Treponema pallidum (syphilis). There were no randomized controlled trials comparing different screening and treatment strategies, and the evidence for the effectiveness of RST is primarily derived from cost-effectiveness models and diagnostic accuracy data. 5. The diagnostic accuracy of on-site RSTs was confirmed through a systematic review of 10 studies, with moderate certainty in the results. All tests were compared to a gold standard of laboratory-based tests combining RPR-positive and TPPAor TPHA-positive results. The evidence linking these data sources was of low certainty. 6. The use of a single on-site RST followed by treatment (Strategy A) or an on-site RST followed by the first dose of treatment if positive, and then an RPR test with further treatment if positive (Strategy C), may result in slightly to moderately higher numbers of people being treated compared to on-site RPR strategies (Strategies B and E). This is true across all prevalence settings, with approximately 4 more treated per 1,000 pregnant women in low-prevalence settings and 20–30 more per 1,000 in higher-prevalence settings. 7. The difference in harm caused by over-treatment is minimal between the single on-site RST (Strategy A) and the single on-site RPR test (Strategy B) in low-prevalence settings (9 more per 1,000 pregnant women with the RPR strategy). However, in higher-prevalence settings, the difference in over-treatment between these strategies may be moderate and favor the RST strategy (approximately 30–50 more per 1,000 pregnant women with the RPR strategy). 8. The difference in missed treatment cases is small between the single on-site RST (Strategy A) and the single on-site RPR test (Strategy B) in low-prevalence settings (approximately 4 more per 1,000 pregnant women with the RPR strategy) but moderate in higher-prevalence settings (25–30 more per 1,000 pregnant women with the RPR strategy). 9. The number of pregnant women screened appears to be slightly higher or similar with the single on-site RST strategy (Strategy A) compared to other strategies, regardless of prevalence settings. The GDG emphasized the importance of minimizing missed syphilis cases due to the severe adverse effects of syphilis in pregnancy, including congenital syphilis and fetal death. 10. Over-treatment, while associated with minor side effects such as gastrointestinal symptoms, was considered acceptable to some extent. However, over-treatment in large proportions of tested women was deemed undesirable. 11. Although there is no direct evidence on the impact of different screening and treatment strategies on partner notification, the GDG agreed that providing a sequence of tests (Strategy C) could increase partner treatment. This is because additional tests may enhance belief in the positive results among tested pregnant women and their partners. 12. Cost-effectiveness modeling showed that total costs per 1,000 women screened were lowest with RPR in Tanzania and Zambia, while RSTs were the cheapest option in Peru due to labor costs associated with RPR. The most cost-effective approach in all prevalence settings was a single on-site RST followed by treatment if positive (Strategy A), though this strategy may cost more in some settings. 13. There were no studies directly measuring the impact of different strategies on equity. However, screening rates achieved with the single on-site RST strategy (Strategy A) appeared slightly higher, regardless of cost, suggesting that such costs may not reduce equity. 14. Health workers and pregnant women were generally satisfied with RSTs, as they reduced clinic visits and were easy to use. On-site tests have been successfully implemented in many countries, though a sequence of on-site tests may be unaffordable in some settings and require adequate provider training. 15. The WHO guidelines recommend benzathine penicillin as the first-line treatment for syphilis in pregnant women. If benzathine penicillin is unavailable, alternative treatments such as erythromycin, ceftriaxone, or azithromycin may be used with caution. However, erythromycin and azithromycin do not cross the placental barrier completely, necessitating treatment of the newborn after delivery. 16. Doxycycline should not be used in pregnant women. Stock-outs of benzathine penicillin should be avoided, as syphilis during pregnancy can lead to severe complications for the fetus or newborn. 17. Countries should conduct high-quality studies to gather local data for adapting these guidelines to their specific STI situations. In the absence of local data, the recommendations in this guideline can be adopted as presented. 18. Decisions on whether to continue the current antenatal syphilis screening algorithm or introduce a new strategy involving treponemal-based RSTs should be based on an assessment of screening coverage, treatment rates, and the quality of the existing testing system. If coverage and treatment rates are below 95%, efforts should be made to address system inadequacies or consider introducing new strategies. 19. Accurate baseline data on syphilis prevalence among pregnant women, based on RPR test results confirmed by TPHA or TPPA, are essential for implementation. Low syphilis prevalence is defined as below 5%, and high prevalence as 5% or above. 20. The single on-site RST strategy (Strategy A) is cost-effective, feasible to implement, and acceptable to key stakeholders. However, the choice of strategy should consider available resources, including laboratory facilities, electricity, and transportation costs for laboratory samples.
